question: What is the minimum and maximum installed capacity allowed for a rooftop solar PV system under net metering in Gujarat?
ground_truth: Under clause 6.2 of the GERC Net Metering Rooftop Solar PV Regulations, 2016, the installed capacity shall not be less than 1 kW and shall not exceed 1 MW.

question: Is a residential consumer in Gujarat limited to 50% of sanctioned load when installing rooftop solar under net metering?
ground_truth: No. The 2016 regulation (clause 6.2) capped capacity at 50% of sanctioned load/contract demand, but as amended (First Amendment, 2017) the 50% cap applies to consumers other than residential consumers; for residential consumers capacity is irrespective of their sanctioned load/contract demand, subject to the 1 kW - 1 MW range.

question: Is banking of energy allowed for rooftop solar net metering in Gujarat, and for how long?
ground_truth: Yes. Under clause 9 of the GERC Net Metering Regulations, 2016, banking of energy is allowed within one billing cycle of the consumer.

question: At what rate does the Gujarat distribution licensee buy excess rooftop solar energy injected by a residential consumer under net metering?
ground_truth: Excess injected electricity in a billing period is purchased by the distribution licensee at the APPC rate determined by GERC for the year in which the rooftop system is commissioned, for the whole life of the system (clause 9 of the 2016 Regulations).

question: Are rooftop solar systems under net metering in Gujarat exempt from wheeling charges and cross subsidy surcharge?
ground_truth: Yes. Clause 12.1 exempts rooftop solar PV systems under net metering from Transmission Charge, Transmission Loss, Wheeling Charge, Wheeling Loss, Cross Subsidy Surcharge and Additional Surcharge.

question: What connectivity charges apply to a 50 kW rooftop solar system in Gujarat?
ground_truth: Under Annexure-III of the GERC Net Metering Regulations, 2016, systems of more than 6 kW up to 100 kW pay INR 10,000 per connection (1-6 kW: INR 1,500; more than 100 kW up to 1 MW: INR 50,000).

question: What is the cap on cumulative rooftop solar capacity at a distribution transformer in Gujarat?
ground_truth: Under clause 5 of the GERC Net Metering Regulations, 2016, cumulative capacity allowed at a particular distribution transformer shall not exceed 65% of the peak capacity of the distribution transformer.

question: Who bears the cost of distribution system strengthening for a 5 kW rooftop solar system in Gujarat after the 2024 amendment?
ground_truth: Under clause 5.1 as substituted by the GERC Fourth Amendment Regulations, 2024 (dated 04.09.2024), the cost of strengthening distribution infrastructure for rooftop systems up to 6 kW is included in the distribution licensee's Annual Revenue Requirement, i.e. not charged to the applicant; above 6 kW system strengthening charges are recovered from the applicant.

question: Under the 2024 amendment in Gujarat, is a technical feasibility study needed for a 8 kW rooftop solar application, and what compensation applies for discom delay?
ground_truth: Per the substituted Regulation 7 (GERC Fourth Amendment, 2024), applications up to 10 kW complete in all respects are deemed accepted without a technical feasibility study; for delay by the licensee without just cause, compensation of not less than five hundred rupees per day of default is payable.

question: What is the maximum capacity of a rooftop renewable energy system relative to sanctioned load in Maharashtra?
ground_truth: Under Regulation 6.2 of the MERC Grid Interactive Rooftop RE Generating Systems Regulations, 2019, capacity shall not exceed the Sanctioned Load (kW) or Contract Demand (kVA) of the consumer; minimum size is 1 kW (Reg 6.1).

question: What is the distribution transformer capacity limit for net metering in Maharashtra?
ground_truth: Regulation 5.2 of MERC 2019 Regulations: cumulative capacity under net metering/net billing on a distribution transformer/feeder shall not exceed 70% of its rated capacity, though the licensee may allow more after a detailed load study.

question: What happens to unadjusted net metering credits at the end of the financial year in Maharashtra?
ground_truth: Under Regulation 11.4(c) of the MERC 2019 Regulations, unadjusted net credited units at the end of each financial year are purchased by the distribution licensee at the Generic Tariff approved by the Commission for that year, within the first month of the following year; carried-forward injected electricity is reset to zero at the start of each settlement period. The First Amendment, 2023 added a proviso to Regulation 11.4(e): if the credit amount keeps increasing at the end of three consecutive financial years, 50% is paid in cash within 60 days and the balance 50% is credited in the second electricity bill.

question: Do small rooftop solar consumers in Maharashtra pay Grid Support Charges?
ground_truth: Regulation 11.5 of MERC 2019 Regulations allows Grid Support Charges on net metering, but consumers of all categories with Sanctioned Load up to 10 kW are exempted from Grid Support Charges.

question: What registration fee does an LT consumer with 15 kW sanctioned load pay for rooftop solar connectivity in Maharashtra?
ground_truth: Under Regulation 9.1 of MERC 2019 Regulations, LT consumers pay Rs. 500 for sanctioned load/contract demand up to 20 kW (Rs 100 for every further 20 kW or part); HT consumers pay Rs 5,000.

question: Does the 1 MW capacity limit apply to net billing arrangements in Maharashtra?
ground_truth: No. An Eligible Consumer is defined with a system capacity less than 1 MW, but the definition (Reg 2.1(j)) provides that in case of Net Billing Arrangement the 1 MW capacity limit shall not apply.

question: Did the 2023 amendment to Maharashtra's rooftop RE regulations introduce gross metering?
ground_truth: Yes. The MERC (Grid Interactive Rooftop RE Generating Systems) (First Amendment) Regulations, 2023 (Statement of Reasons dated 16 November 2023) added Gross Metering arrangements (Regulation 3.1(c)) and related provisions such as the Gross Metering Agreement.

question: What is the current net metering capacity limit in Rajasthan?
ground_truth: By RERC suo-motu order dated 07.02.2024, net metering applies to loads up to one megawatt (1 MW) or up to the sanctioned load/contract demand, whichever is lower, for all consumer categories - raised from the earlier limit of 500 kW set by the suo-motu order of 07.09.2021.

question: Can a consumer in Rajasthan install a renewable system larger than their sanctioned load under the DREGS Regulations?
ground_truth: No. Regulation 7.2 of the RERC DREGS Regulations, 2021 says the maximum capacity at an eligible consumer's premises shall not exceed 100% of the Sanctioned Load/Contract Demand.

question: What is the distribution transformer capacity limit for distributed renewable systems in Rajasthan?
ground_truth: Regulation 6.1 of the RERC DREGS Regulations, 2021: cumulative capacity at a distribution transformer shall not exceed 50% of its capacity (not applicable to HT consumers who installed their own transformer).

question: How is excess net metering export by a domestic consumer paid for in Rajasthan, and what happens for non-domestic consumers?
ground_truth: Under Regulation 12.6.1 of RERC DREGS Regulations, 2021, excess export by domestic consumers is purchased at the weighted average tariff of large-scale solar projects of 5 MW and more discovered through competitive bidding in the last financial year, credited in the next billing cycle; for non-domestic consumers net surplus at the end of the billing period lapses with no payment.

question: Did RERC impose restrictions on drawal of banked solar units during peak hours or mandatory storage for rooftop solar in 2024?
ground_truth: No. In the 07.02.2024 order RERC noted discom requests for peak-hour drawal restrictions, charges and compulsory storage but held it would not be appropriate to impose them at the present level of rooftop penetration, while it may consider them in future.

question: What is the KERC approved tariff for 1 kW to 10 kW domestic rooftop solar projects for FY24?
ground_truth: KERC order dated 01.06.2023: Rs. 4.50 per unit without capital subsidy and Rs. 2.97 per unit with capital subsidy for grid-connected solar rooftop PV of 1 kW to 10 kW for domestic consumers.

question: What tariff applies to a 500 kW solar rooftop project in Karnataka under the FY24 order, and for how long is the PPA?
ground_truth: Rs. 3.74 per unit for grid connected solar rooftop PV projects of 1 kW to 2000 kW (excluding 1-10 kW), applicable to PPAs entered on or after 01.04.2023; PPA tenure is the life of the project, 25 years.

question: Does KERC levy grid support charges on solar rooftop PV installations?
ground_truth: No. KERC decided not to levy any grid support charges on SRTPV installations until it determines them after conducting necessary studies (FY24 tariff order dated 01.06.2023).

question: What capacity utilisation factor did KERC adopt for solar plants in the FY24 generic tariff?
ground_truth: KERC adopted a CUF of 19% for solar plants, both ground mounted and SRTPV.

question: Which metering mechanism applies to domestic and non-domestic LT rooftop solar consumers in Tamil Nadu under the current order?
ground_truth: Per TANGEDCO's summary of TNERC GISS Order No. 8 of 2021 dated 22.10.2021, net metering is adopted for domestic consumers and net feed-in for all other LT consumer categories; HT capacities of 1-999 kW are under net feed-in.

question: Under the proposed 2024 Tamil Nadu regulations, what capacity range is allowed for gross metering?
ground_truth: The DRAFT TNERC GISS Regulations, 2024 (clause 4.4) propose gross metering for consumers other than LT up to 150 kW and generators, with minimum size above 150 kW up to a maximum of 999 kW. This is a draft, not in force.

question: What happens to surplus net metering credit at the end of the settlement period under the draft Tamil Nadu 2024 regulations?
ground_truth: Under clause 6.1 of the DRAFT TNERC GISS Regulations, 2024, net surplus units available at the end of the settlement period lapse. This is a draft proposal.

question: What is the minimum contracted demand for a consumer to use Green Energy Open Access under the central rules?
ground_truth: Under the Electricity (Promoting Renewable Energy Through Green Energy Open Access) Rules, 2022, an entity is a consumer with contracted demand or sanctioned load of 100 kW or more; captive consumers have no load limitation.

question: What banking provisions apply to green energy open access consumers under the Ministry of Power rules?
ground_truth: Rule 8 of the GEOA Rules, 2022: banking permitted at least monthly on payment of charges fixed by the Commission; banked quantum at least 30% of total monthly consumption from the licensee; banked credit cannot be carried forward and must be adjusted in the same month.

question: Compare the distribution transformer capacity limits for rooftop solar in Gujarat and Maharashtra.
ground_truth: Gujarat: cumulative capacity shall not exceed 65% of the transformer's peak capacity (GERC 2016, clause 5). Maharashtra: shall not exceed 70% of rated capacity, more allowed after a load study (MERC 2019, Reg 5.2).

question: What is the maximum net metering capacity in Gujarat versus Rajasthan?
ground_truth: Gujarat: up to 1 MW (not less than 1 kW), GERC 2016 clause 6.2. Rajasthan: up to 1 MW or sanctioned load/contract demand whichever is lower, per RERC order of 07.02.2024 (raised from 500 kW).

question: What is the wheeling charge in paise per kWh for open access solar in Karnataka for FY2026?
ground_truth: ABSTAIN - the indexed documents do not contain Karnataka FY2026 wheeling charges.

question: What is the net metering limit for rooftop solar in Kerala?
ground_truth: ABSTAIN - Kerala is not covered by the indexed documents.
